🟠 Nine Major Firms Launch $15M Bitcoin Security Consortium

BlackRock, Coinbase, Strategy, Fidelity Digital Assets, Anchorage Digital, ARK Invest, Block, Blockstream, and Galaxy have formed the Bitcoin Security Consortium, pledging $15 million over three years to fund open-source developers and advance quantum-resistant security research for the Bitcoin network.

Announced July 23, the consortium will direct funding independently, with members taking no role in Bitcoin governance or protocol decisions. Research priorities include post-quantum cryptography and long-term network resilience against potential future quantum-computing threats.

The initiative reflects growing institutional concern over quantum computing's long-term risk to Bitcoin's cryptographic foundations, with participants spanning Wall Street asset managers, crypto exchanges, and infrastructure providers.

🗡 “Never Vance”: The GOP Eats Its Own Early

JD Vance hasn’t even said he’s running in 2028, and his own party is already running a soft launch of “Never Vance.”

Inside the GOP, the vice president is taking fire from a flank that used to wait until succession was formal: influencers, neoconservatives and pro‑Israel commentators are hammering him for trying to negotiate a peace framework with Iran and for sounding “too moderate” on Israel in a three‑hour Joe Rogan interview. 

The attacks brand him “unfit,” accuse him — without evidence — of freelancing foreign policy behind Trump’s back, and compare him to Obama and Bernie Sanders. Allies say the timing is the tell: two years before the primary, with Vance still the polling front‑runner and Rubio slowly gaining ground as the business‑friendly alternative.

Vance’s camp is leaning into the backlash. They argue that the online barrage is “obviously” at least partly coordinated, point to charts showing his favorability among Republicans tracking Trump almost exactly, and frame the noise as proof that “Washington establishment voices” and neocon donors hate him — which, in a populist primary, is supposed to be a badge of honor. 

The vice president himself has gone full anti‑influence narrative, citing a Time report on a pro‑Israel operation run by a former Trump digital aide and telling Rogan his answer to paid smears is “go to hell, I represent Americans first.”

The split with the old guard is real. Pence spent four years refusing to show daylight between himself and Trump until the January 6 break; Harris absorbed quiet Democratic panic about succession but little open revolt. 

Vance is dealing with something different: a public ideological knife fight over Iran, Israel and foreign wars, with Trump on record saying they’re “philosophically a little bit different” on Iran and that Vance was “maybe less enthusiastic about going” to war, even as the vice president now defends the strikes and says Iran must never get a bomb.

Underneath the memes and “Never Vance” slogans is a serious question: who owns the post‑Trump GOP’s foreign policy — the war‑skeptical populist vice president, or the donors and media figures who still want the party to sound like 2004 on Israel and Iran? The knives are out because everyone knows the answer will decide more than just one primary.
